engagement.coverage_declaration: Read end to end, statically: all four Java sources (121 lines) and README.md. Nothing was compiled, executed or fuzzed — the target is read-only and no network was used, so no allocation was observed failing and no StackOverflowError was produced; every claim below is source-level. The scope contains no caller: nothing in it constructs a ValueDecoder or a FrameReader, opens a socket, or shows the thread and heap settings the process runs under, so reachability of the decoder from a remote peer is argued from the code's own documentation, not observed. Surfaces not covered because they are absent from the scope: encoding/serialisation side, transport and TLS, authentication, framing above readFrame, and any consumer of the decoded Map/List.

findings.title: Blob length from the wire sizes the allocation, guarded only against the cast wrapping
findings.evidence: readBlob reads four bytes from the peer and widens them: `long declared = in.readInt() & 0xFFFFFFFFL;` (line 19). The only test is `if (declared >= Integer.MAX_VALUE) throw new MalformedFrameException("blob too large");` (lines 20-22) — a cast-safety test, not a limit: it rejects exactly one value out of 2^32 and lets every length up to 2,147,483,646 through. `byte[] blob = new byte[(int) declared];` (line 23) then commits up to ~2 GiB of heap, and only `in.readFully(blob)` (line 24) discovers there are no such bytes. Neither `Settings.MAX_FRAME_BYTES` (131,072) nor `Settings.MAX_STRING_BYTES` (65,535) is read anywhere in this method; the sibling `readText` (lines 29-33) shows the codebase's own intended discipline — `if (declared > Settings.MAX_STRING_BYTES) throw ...` before `new byte[declared]` — and readBlob omits it. Reproduction, if the target were runnable: feed the decoder the five bytes `78 7F FF FF FE` (tag 'x' = 0x78, then length 0x7FFFFFFE) via readValue.
findings.impact: A peer, or anyone who can inject or tamper with frames on the connection, makes the decoding process commit an arbitrary heap allocation up to ~2 GiB with a five-byte message and no credential. The result is OutOfMemoryError or heavy GC pressure in the JVM that runs the decoder — process-wide, so it also takes down connections and work unrelated to the attacker's own. The bytes never have to exist: the damage is done by the allocation, before readFully can fail. Repeating it is as cheap as reconnecting.
findings.preconditions: The DataInputStream handed to the ValueDecoder constructor carries bytes chosen by the remote peer — which is what FrameReader's javadoc ("Reads one frame off the socket and hands its body to the value decoder") and Settings' javadoc ("Limits the peer cannot change") describe. No authentication step exists anywhere in the scope, so nothing gates the decoder. Default JVM heap; on a heap already smaller than the declared length the allocation fails immediately, which is the same denial of service.
findings.recommendation: Bound the length against a value the peer does not set, before the array exists: compare `declared` to `Settings.MAX_FRAME_BYTES` (or to a dedicated MAX_BLOB_BYTES) and to the bytes actually remaining in the frame, and throw MalformedFrameException when it exceeds either — the shape `readText` already uses. Keep the `>= Integer.MAX_VALUE` test as the cast guard it is; it is not a substitute. Better still at root-cause level: give the decoder the frame body it is meant to parse (a byte[] or a bounded stream carrying `remaining()`), so no field length can ever exceed what has already been read, and grow into a ByteArrayOutputStream rather than pre-sizing from a declared count. The same rule then covers every future value type without each one re-deriving it.
findings.inference: That the stream reaching ValueDecoder carries peer-controlled bytes. The scope contains no call site: nothing in it constructs a ValueDecoder, and the DataInputStream arrives through the constructor (lines 14-16). The link is read from FrameReader's class javadoc and Settings' "Limits the peer cannot change", not from observed wiring. Everything else — untrusted length, absent bound, allocation before read — is read directly in the file.

triage.reason: The only candidate control is FrameReader.readFrame's `length > Settings.MAX_FRAME_BYTES` test (FrameReader.java:16), and it cannot save this sink for two independent reasons. First, it bounds a different object: it caps the body byte[] that readFrame returns, while ValueDecoder holds its own DataInputStream (ValueDecoder.java:12-16) and no code in scope connects the two. Second, even if the decoder were fed a 131,072-byte body, `new byte[(int) declared]` on line 23 runs before `in.readFully(blob)` on line 24 — the allocation is sized by the declaration, never by the bytes available, so a bound on the bytes available arrives after the array already exists. A control the sink does not consult, in a layer the sink does not pass through, is not this rule.

`declared` is the four bytes returned by `in.readInt()` on line 19, widened by `& 0xFFFFFFFFL`. It is read straight off the peer's stream, passes through no allowlist, and the only test applied to it (line 20) narrows its domain by exactly one value.

The scope names the second principal itself: Settings.java:3 says "Limits the peer cannot change" and FrameReader.java:6 says the frame is read "off the socket". A peer across a socket is a different trust domain from the process decoding its bytes, which is why the limits exist at all.

findings.limits: Establishes an unbounded attacker-sized allocation in code, not a crash observed: nothing was compiled or run, so the heap ceiling of the deployment and whether an OutOfMemoryError kills the process or only the decoding thread are unknown. It does not establish that a remote peer reaches this method — no call site ships in the scope (see `inference`). It says nothing about the encoding side, and the severity assumes the decoder runs in a process that does other work; in a single-purpose short-lived process the impact is smaller.

findings.title: Mutual recursion between readValue, readMap and readList carries no depth counter
findings.evidence: The cycle is closed and unmetered: `readValue` (line 56) dispatches tag 'M' to `readMap` (line 61) and tag 'A' to `readList` (line 62); `readMap` calls `readValue` on line 42 and `readList` calls it on line 51. No signature in the file carries a depth parameter, no field counts nesting, and no constant in Settings.java names a depth. The attacker pays about three bytes per level: the tag byte `41` ('A') plus the two-byte entry count `00 01` from `in.readUnsignedShort()` (line 49) buys one more frame of `readValue` + `readList`. A 131,072-byte frame — the largest FrameReader will accept — therefore encodes on the order of 43,000 nesting levels, and a stream not bounded by FrameReader encodes any depth at all. The per-level cost is the same shape the procedure names as the neighbouring case of the allocation, in the same file.
findings.impact: A peer denies service with a small, cheap, unauthenticated message: repeating `41 00 01` until the frame budget runs out drives the decoding thread into StackOverflowError. StackOverflowError is an Error, not the IOException the protocol's own MalformedFrameException (MalformedFrameException.java:5) trains callers to catch, so it escapes the parser's error handling and unwinds the thread — at best killing the connection handler, at worst propagating past a catch that only covers IOException and leaving whatever the thread owned in a half-updated state.
findings.preconditions: Same as F-001: the DataInputStream reaching the decoder carries peer-chosen bytes, and no authentication precedes decoding anywhere in the scope. Reaching StackOverflowError requires the thread's stack to be smaller than the nesting the frame budget allows — true for the default JVM thread stack (512 KiB-1 MiB) against ~43,000 levels of two frames each, and more true for any thread created with a smaller stack.
findings.recommendation: Thread a depth argument through the recursive entry points — `readValue(int depth)`, `readMap(int depth)`, `readList(int depth)` — increment it at each descent, and throw MalformedFrameException past a configured maximum declared beside the existing limits in Settings (a protocol that needs more than a handful of levels is a protocol that should say so). Add the aggregate bound the depth cap does not give: a running count of values decoded per frame, so 65,535 sibling entries at every level cannot exhaust memory breadth-first either. Keep the public one-argument methods as wrappers that start at depth zero, so no caller can enter the cycle unmetered.
findings.inference: The same single link as F-001: that the stream reaching ValueDecoder carries peer-controlled bytes, which the scope documents (FrameReader.java:6, Settings.java:3) but does not wire up in code. The recursion cycle, the absent depth parameter and the per-level byte cost are all read directly in ValueDecoder.java.

triage.reason: The candidate control is again Settings.MAX_FRAME_BYTES enforced at FrameReader.java:16. Taken at its most favourable — the decoder fed a body capped at 131,072 bytes — it bounds the depth at roughly 131,072 / 3 = ~43,000 levels, which is far past the default JVM thread stack. A limit that permits tens of thousands of frames of recursion does not bound the recursion, and here it is not even reached: the decoder reads from its own DataInputStream and no code in scope routes the frame body into it.

Both values that drive the descent come off the wire: the tag byte from `in.readUnsignedByte()` (line 57) selects 'M' or 'A', and the entry counts from `in.readUnsignedShort()` (lines 40 and 49) decide how many children each level has. Neither is constrained by anything the process controls.

Same boundary as F-001, named by the target itself: Settings.java:3 "Limits the peer cannot change" and FrameReader.java:6 "off the socket". The bytes that choose the nesting depth come from the peer, across the socket.

findings.limits: Establishes an unmetered recursion cycle and the attacker's per-level cost from source; it does not establish the exact depth at which this JVM overflows, because nothing was compiled or run and the deployment's thread stack size is not in the scope. It does not establish that a remote peer reaches the decoder (see `inference`), nor what a caller does with a StackOverflowError — no caller ships in the scope. Breadth is not covered by this finding beyond the note in the recommendation: 65,535 entries per container is a separate multiplier that was not measured.
